title: 1 Chronicles 1:17–27
context: The list now turns to Shem, then narrows from Shem to Abram, who is also called Abraham. Verses 17–23 follow the Shemite table in Genesis 10:21–29, and verses 24–27 follow the straight line of Genesis 11:10–26, again with names only and without the years of Genesis 11. Differences from those chapters should be named, not harmonized. In 1:17 Uz, Hul, Gether, and Meshech are listed among the sons of Shem, whereas Genesis 10:22–23 names them as the sons of Aram, and the last name is Meshech here and Mash there. In 1:22 Ebal appears where Genesis 10:28 has Obal. The Peleg notice, “for in his days the earth was divided”, is shared with Genesis 10:25 and is not expanded here. The unit closes by identifying Abram as Abraham, and so prepares the next section, in which Abraham’s own sons will be named. Both traditions take the Chronicler to be tracing, through Shem, the line that will lead to Israel, while still leaving Shem’s broader family on the page.

verses.text: The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, Aram, Uz, Hul, Gether, and Meshech.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, Aram, Uz, Hul, Gether, and Meshech.” Genesis 10:22 lists Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, and Aram as Shem’s sons, and Genesis 10:23 then names Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash as Aram’s sons. Here the last four are listed with Shem, and the last name is Meshech, not Mash. The difference of arrangement and spelling should be left as a difference.

Arminian readers note the parallel without inventing a single reconstructed family tree the text does not give.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise refuse to force 1:17 and Genesis 10:22–23 into one official form. The verse still places Shem’s family in the Chronicler’s world table.

Both traditions read this Shemite stretch as the narrowing of the world’s families toward Abraham, still without allegory and without forcing the Genesis parallels into one spelling or one arrangement.

verses.text: Arpachshad became the father of Shelah, and Shelah became the father of Eber.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Arpachshad became the father of Shelah, and Shelah became the father of Eber.” The same two steps stand in Genesis 10:24 and in the dated line of Genesis 11:12–15. Chronicles gives the birth line without the years.

Arminian readers take Shelah and Eber as real links in a historical chain, the ordinary means by which the line is kept.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same compressed parallel. The promise line moves through Arpachshad, Shelah, and Eber, as Genesis had already said, now in the Chronicler’s shorter style.

Both traditions read this Shemite stretch as the narrowing of the world’s families toward Abraham, still without allegory and without forcing the Genesis parallels into one spelling or one arrangement.

verses.text: To Eber were born two sons: the name of the one was Peleg, for in his days the earth was divided; and his brother’s name was Joktan.
verses.arminianNotes:
Eber’s two sons are named: Peleg, “for in his days the earth was divided”, and his brother Joktan. Genesis 10:25 has the same etymology and the same two names. The present verse does not explain the division further, and the earlier Genesis notes already treat that phrase with caution.

Arminian readers let the notice stand as the text gives it, a named brother and a remembered division, not a cue for allegory.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the parallel in view and decline to settle, here, what the division of the earth was. The Chronicler is still moving from Shem toward Abraham.

Both traditions read this Shemite stretch as the narrowing of the world’s families toward Abraham, still without allegory and without forcing the Genesis parallels into one spelling or one arrangement.

verses.text: Joktan became the father of Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah,
verses.arminianNotes:
Joktan’s sons begin: “Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah,” matching Genesis 10:26, with the list continuing in the next verses.

Arminian readers receive these names as a real branching of Shem’s family, recorded even though Israel’s later line will run through Peleg, not through Joktan.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the Chronicler following Genesis 10:26 in naming Joktan’s house, so that Shem is more than a single straight path.

Both traditions read this Shemite stretch as the narrowing of the world’s families toward Abraham, still without allegory and without forcing the Genesis parallels into one spelling or one arrangement.

verses.arminianNotes:
The Joktan list continues: “Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah,” the same three names, in the same order, as Genesis 10:27.

Arminian readers keep the verse as a simple continuation of the family record, not as a map that must be filled with certain modern sites.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also refuse uncertain identifications. The names stand in parallel with Genesis 10:27, and that is enough for this line.

Both traditions read this Shemite stretch as the narrowing of the world’s families toward Abraham, still without allegory and without forcing the Genesis parallels into one spelling or one arrangement.

verses.arminianNotes:
Next are “Ebal, Abimael, Sheba,”. Genesis 10:28 has Obal, Abimael, and Sheba. The first name differs: Ebal here, Obal there. The variant should be named neutrally, without a forced explanation.

Arminian readers can hold the two spellings side by side and still read a genuine family list, not a riddle.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also decline to harmonize Ebal and Obal. The parallel is Genesis 10:28; the difference remains, and the list goes on.

Both traditions read this Shemite stretch as the narrowing of the world’s families toward Abraham, still without allegory and without forcing the Genesis parallels into one spelling or one arrangement.

verses.text: Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab. All these were the sons of Joktan.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Joktan names close: “Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab. All these were the sons of Joktan.” The sentence matches the close of Genesis 10:29. Chronicles does not add the eastern dwelling notice of Genesis 10:30.

Arminian readers take the summary as a historical close of this branch, then the Chronicler will return to the narrower line.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the same ending formula and the omitted geography. Joktan’s sons have been catalogued, as in Genesis 10, and the straight line from Shem can now be restated.

Both traditions read this Shemite stretch as the narrowing of the world’s families toward Abraham, still without allegory and without forcing the Genesis parallels into one spelling or one arrangement.

verses.arminianNotes:
A new, shorter chain begins: “Shem, Arpachshad, Shelah,”. This is the style of verses 1–4, and it follows the direct descent of Genesis 11:10–15, without years.

Arminian readers hear the Chronicler returning from Joktan’s many sons to the line that will reach Abraham, a real narrowing, not an allegory of election’s shape.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the same return to the Genesis 11 line. Shem, Arpachshad, and Shelah are restated so that the path to Abram is clear.

Both traditions read this Shemite stretch as the narrowing of the world’s families toward Abraham, still without allegory and without forcing the Genesis parallels into one spelling or one arrangement.

verses.arminianNotes:
The chain continues: “Eber, Peleg, Reu,” the next three names in Genesis 11:16–21, again without the dated notices of that chapter.

Arminian readers take the three as successive links already known from Genesis 11, listed here so that the royal story still stands inside that older family.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read a compressed form of Genesis 11. The line is being carried, name by name, toward Abraham.

Both traditions read this Shemite stretch as the narrowing of the world’s families toward Abraham, still without allegory and without forcing the Genesis parallels into one spelling or one arrangement.

verses.arminianNotes:
“Serug, Nahor, Terah” complete the pre-Abraham names of Genesis 11:22–26. Genesis also names Abram’s brothers at Terah’s point; this verse gives only the straight chain.

Arminian readers let the shorter form stand. The Chronicler is not retelling Terah’s household; he is arriving at Abram.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note what is not repeated from Genesis 11:26–32. The three names are enough, in this style, to reach the next verse’s identification.

Both traditions read this Shemite stretch as the narrowing of the world’s families toward Abraham, still without allegory and without forcing the Genesis parallels into one spelling or one arrangement.

verses.arminianNotes:
The unit ends: “Abram (also called Abraham).” The Chronicler makes the identification explicit, joining the Genesis 11 name Abram to the name by which the father of Isaac and Ishmael is known in the stories that follow.

Arminian readers hear a historical hinge, not a symbol. The man named in the Shemite line is Abraham, and his sons will now be listed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same close as the turning point of the opening genealogies. The world’s families have been named; the line has arrived at Abraham, and the next unit will name his offspring.

Both traditions read this Shemite stretch as the narrowing of the world’s families toward Abraham, still without allegory and without forcing the Genesis parallels into one spelling or one arrangement.
